Mark Robbins A BS in psychology prepares students for a wide variety of career options.
According to the website of the American Psychological Association ( https://www.apa.org/ed/precollege/psn/2018/01/bachelors-degree ), about 25 percent of psychology baccalaureates go to graduate school in psychology, about 18 percent go on for more education but not in psychology, and 57 percent are workforce graduates (Lin, Christidis & Stamm, 2017).
The BS degree prepares graduates especially well to apply to doctoral or other research-oriented advanced degrees in Psychology or other fields.

For those who do not wish to obtain an advanced degree, there are many job opportunities.

The BS degree with its focus on methodology, scientific writing, and statistical analysis especially trains graduates for any type of position requiring analytic, scientific writing, or data analytic skills, such as data base design analyst, research assistant, systems analyst, technical writer, information specialist, or data base manager.

The Occupational Outlook Handbook of the Bureau of Labor ( https://www.bls.gov/ooh/field-of- degree/psychology/psychology-field-of-degree.htm ) indicates that the median salary for those with a degree in Psychology is $50,000 and that 60% are employed in occupations requiring at least a bachelor's degree.

The University of Delaware offers a BS in Neuroscience but not Psychology.

Summary of Proposed Change: A change in department name is proposed from "Chemical Engineering" to "Chemical, Biomolecular, and Materials Engineering" to better reflect the fields chemical engineering students enter after graduation, the research expertise in our department, and the content in our courses and minors. The name change will also provide a platform for department growth and aid recruiting efforts at the undergraduate, graduate, and faculty levels. Course codes and names of degrees will not change. V. 24.01.26 RATIONALE There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed name change. 1.
Explain why the change of department name is being proposed.
The proposed new name of "Chemical, Biomolecular, and Materials Engineering" accurately reflects the career and technological fields that graduates enter and the research and scholarly expertise of the department faculty.
For example, the department has many graduates working at Amgen, which is a biotechnology company producing biological molecules (i.e., biomolecules), as well as Toray Plastics America, which produces polymeric materials.
The new name also reflects topics that are taught in our courses and the newly formed department Minor in Materials Engineering.
An additional Minor in Biochemical Engineering has been proposed (expected launch in Spring 2025) and a minor in Pharmaceutical Manufacturing and Formulation (includes biomolecular topics) is offered by the Department of Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Sciences for c hemical engineering majors.

The proposed new name aligns with similar department names of URI's peer and aspiring institutions, which include terms such as "bioengineering", "biomedical", and "biological engineering" in their names preceded by the term "chemical".
Changing the department name at URI is expected to make us more competitive in undergraduate student recruiting and, coupled with the new name reflecting our research expertise, more competitive at recruiting graduate s tudents and faculty.
INSTITUTIONAL ROLE The department name change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution. 1.
Explain how the name change is consistent with published role and mission of the institution, and how it is related to institutional planning.
As with our current name, the new name will continue to align with the role and mission of the institution in providing high-quality education and solving the world's most challenging problems (the new name explicitly extends this to biomolecules and materials).

It also aligns with institutional planning, providing new opportunities to increase student recruiting, to create new degree and/or certificate programs, and to pursue interdisciplinary collaboration (funding agencies/proposal review panels link department names to expertise). 2.
Explain how the organizational change impacts other units and programs within the institution.
Have you communicated with the other units and programs and have any concerns been raised relative to the organizational change?
Describe the concerns.
The proposed name change was formally presented to the department chairs in the College of Engineering and no concerns were raised - they were collectively enthusiastic.
The potential for the most overlap is with the Biomedical Engineering program in the Department of Electrical, Computer, and Biomedical Engineering.
The CHE chair discussed the name change with the program lead for Biomedical Engineering and the only concern was with the abbreviation, CHE changing to CBME. "BME" is the abbreviation for Biomedical Engineering and the BME lead thought this could lead to confusion during registration.

After explaining that the course codes would remain "CHE" there was no longer a concern.
